messages.author: e7a71d967e60bb41
messages.subject: Cleaning up Boxplot
parts:
Dear All,
I need to generate a boxplot representing about 60 different distributions.
Please see the snippet below with artificial data which should give you
a pretty good idea of the kind of plot I want to generate (from what I
learned from the ggplot2 book and http://tinyurl.com/cex-axis)


library(ggplot2)
set.seed(1234)

y<-rnorm(60*100)
x<-rep(seq(60)+200,100)


my_data <- cbind(x,y)
my_data <- as.data.frame(my_data)
my_data$x <- factor(my_data$x)

a <- qplot(x,y, data=my_data, geom="boxplot", xlab="Number of Visitors",
ylab="Number of Infected Distribution")

a <- a+ opts(axis.title.x = theme_text(size = 30))
a <- a+ opts(axis.title.y = theme_text(size = 30, angle=90))
a <- a+ opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(size=15, colour="gray"))
a <- a+ opts(axis.text.y = theme_text(size=15, colour="gray"))

pdf(file="boxplot_by_ggplot.pdf",width = 28, height = 10)

print(a)
dev.off()


There are a few things I cannot fix in this otherwise decent-looking
boxplot.

(1) How can I move the axis labels (I mean the numbers along each axis,
I call axis title the text along the x and y axis telling what is being
plotted) a bit further away from the axis ticks?
(2) How can I add a horizontal segment at the top (bottom) of each
line giving the 95th (5th) quantile?
(3) In axis.text.x I would like to keep the default color, which I guess
to be gray, but there must be a way to tell it to use the default (maybe
I should not use theme_text at all, but other attempts of mine did not
work). **
(4) This is something I have already asked, but I'll give it another
try: how can I get rid the outliers in the resulting plot and have the y
axis adjusted to the new range of the plotted data?
(5)In general, any suggestions about how to change this large boxplot
into something suitable for publication is very appreciated.

Many thanks

Lorenzo

messages.author: b756a7daa2c2aa6d
messages.subject: Re: Cleaning up Boxplot
parts:
> (4) This is something I have already asked, but I'll give it another
> try: how can I get rid the outliers in the resulting plot and have the y
> axis adjusted to the new range of the plotted data?

It sounds to me like you don't actually want a boxplot, you want
something that shares some basic similarities with a boxplot but has
some important differences (e.g. it doesn't show the full range of the
data). This basically means that you need to compute the statistics
yourself and then assemble the necessary layers to create the plot
that you want.

The following code should get you started:

qs <- ddply(my_data, "x", function(df)
quantile(df$y, c(0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95)))

names(qs) <- c("x", "q5", "q25", "q50", "q75", "q95")

ggplot(qs, aes(x)) +
geom_crossbar(aes(y = q50, ymin = q25, ymax = q75)) +
geom_crossbar(aes(y = q95, ymin = q95, ymax = q95)) +
geom_crossbar(aes(y = q5, ymin = q5, ymax = q5))


Hadley

--

Dear Hadley,
Thanks a lot for your suggestions. I think I finally managed to get on
top of this 'problem'. I would say that what I am after is still a
boxplot, though there are no outliers there.
In case it is of interest for anyone else on the list, here is a little
code snippet

rm(list=ls())

limits <- aes(ymax = q25 , ymin=q5)
limits2 <- aes(ymax = q95 , ymin=q75)

b <- ggplot(qs, aes(x)) +

geom_crossbar(aes(y = q50, ymin = q25, ymax = q75)) +
geom_crossbar(aes(y = q95, ymin = q95, ymax = q95)) +

geom_crossbar(aes(y = q5, ymin = q5, ymax = q5))+

geom_errorbar(limits) +
geom_errorbar(limits2)
## geom_vline(aes(xintercept=x, ymin = -1, ymax = 1))

pdf(file="boxplot_by_ggplot_hadley_suggestion.pdf",width = 28, height = 10)

print(b)
dev.off()


Many thanks

Lorenzo

> of this 'problem'. I would say that what I am after is still a boxplot,
> though there are no outliers there.

Your plot is pretty similar to a boxplot, but I'd avoid calling it
that because it has some important differences. For example, if
someone thought they were looking at a boxplot and didn't know that
the outliers had been removed, they might draw the conclusion that
there were no outliers in the dataset. But then I'm an academic so
I'm paid to be precise ;)

Hadley
